A total of 43 Mar-M247 deposits were printed, including 24 single-layer and 19 multi-layer builds.

The CNN-based surrogate model was able to predict melt pool width, depth, and height with an average relative error of less than 20% compared to the high-fidelity CFD simulations and experimental measurements.

The paper introduces four dissimilarity scores to quantify differences in microstructural features: chord length distribution, orientation distribution function, grain growth direction spread, and two-point spatial statistics.
The dissimilarity scores were used in a Bayesian optimization framework to automatically calibrate the parameters of the microstructure simulation model.

The framework combines in-situ data collection, high-fidelity melt pool simulation, machine learning-based surrogate modeling, physics-based microstructure simulation, and statistical quantification of microstructural differences.
The coaxial optical camera used in the experiments had a resolution of 1440 x 1080 pixels and recorded images at 78 frames per second.
The laser powder DED system used a 2 kW, 1030 nm Ytterbium laser to melt the Mar-M247 powder in an inert argon atmosphere.
The microstructure simulation was based on a cellular automata finite element (CAFE) framework, which captured key features like grain morphology and texture.
The high-fidelity melt pool simulation was performed using computational fluid dynamics (CFD) modeling.
The machine learning-based surrogate model was trained using melt pool images from in-situ data and corresponding melt pool dimensions from the CFD simulations.

The proposed framework aims to enable adaptive microstructure control and strengthen the connection between process parameters and final material properties in directed energy deposition additive manufacturing.
The statistical framework for microstructure quantification provides a more comprehensive and reproducible way to compare microstructures beyond just scalar metrics like grain size.

The hybrid approach of combining machine learning and physics-based simulations addresses the limitations of previous methods that relied solely on experimental data or simulation data that may not be representative of actual in-situ conditions.
The paper mentions plans for future collaboration to link the process-microstructure-property relationships to part-level performance simulation.
The experiments were conducted at the Manufacturing Demonstration Facility (MDF) of the Oak Ridge National Laboratory.
